front.title: PACE: Protocol for Agent Communication Exchange

abstract.t: This document defines the Protocol for Agent Communication Exchange (PACE), a session protocol for AI agent communication over Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT). PACE provides session lifecycle management, multi-modal data exchange, agent identity verification, and delegated authorization within MOQT's publish/subscribe model, supporting point-to-point and point-to-multipoint topologies through relay infrastructure.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: AI agents are autonomous software systems that interact with other agents and tools to complete tasks. As agent communication expands across the Internet, it requires: verifiable agent identity independent of users, capability discovery and collaboration across network boundaries, multi-modal data exchange (text, audio, video) with session management, and delegated authorization across agent chains.

This document defines the Protocol for Agent Communication Exchange (PACE), a session layer over Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT) . PACE enables diverse agent protocols to leverage MOQT's publish/subscribe model, relay-based fan-out, built-in prioritization, and efficient multiplexing over QUIC.

li.t: Session Lifecycle: Timed sessions with establishment, update, suspension, and termination.
Multi-Modal: Concurrent real-time media, chat, and operations.
Scalable: Relay-based fan-out with failure recovery.
Flexible Topologies: Point-to-point and point-to-multipoint.
Agent Identity: Authentication independent of user identity with delegated authorization.
Protocol Agnostic: Usable by A2A, MCP, and custom protocols.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Architecture Overview
section.t: The PACE architecture layers as follows:

section.name: MOQT as Session Substrate
section.t: Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT) is a publish/subscribe protocol over QUIC providing:

li.t: Hierarchical Namespaces: Content addressed by namespace tuples, enabling prefix-based routing and caching
Relay Fan-Out: Publishers connect once; relays distribute to all subscribers without direct peer connections
Low Latency: QUIC 0-RTT, stream multiplexing, priority (0-255)
Fault Tolerance: Relay caching enables recovery from disconnections

section.t: Agents connect to MOQT relays which handle subscription matching, fan-out, and object caching. Relays MAY be organized hierarchically for geographic locality.

section.name: Namespace Organization
section.t: PACE uses MOQT's hierarchical namespace for routing, isolation, and multiplexing. MOQT addresses content using a namespace tuple (an ordered sequence of string fields) combined with a track name. PACE organizes all communication into three namespace scopes defined in the following subsections.

section.name: Agent Namespace
section.t: This is an agent's persistent identity on the relay network. Each agent publishes the following tracks:

li.t: "card" — Agent Card containing capabilities, identity claims, authentication schemes, and MOQT connectivity information
"inbox" — Incoming session invitations from other agents; each object contains a session-id and the inviting agent's identifier

section.t: The common prefix ("pace", "agents") enables SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE-based discovery of all agents on the network. See for the complete discovery flow.

section.name: Session Communication Namespace
section.t: A session-id is a shared UUID representing a collaboration context — it is not scoped to or owned by any single agent. Any agent can generate a session-id and invite others to collaborate under it. When multiple agents participate in a session, they each publish tracks under their own agent namespace using the same session-id.

When an agent creates or joins a session, it MUST issue PUBLISH_NAMESPACE on its session namespace (("pace","agents",{agent-id},{session-id})) to enable the relay to route subscriptions to it. This is a separate PUBLISH_NAMESPACE from the agent-level one — MOQT requires an explicit PUBLISH_NAMESPACE for each namespace a publisher wants subscriptions routed to.

To receive messages from a peer within a session, an agent issues SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE on that peer's session namespace (("pace","agents",{peer-agent-id},{session-id})). The relay matches this against the peer's PUBLISH_NAMESPACE and routes subscriptions accordingly.
Each agent in a session publishes the following tracks:

li.t: "ctrl" — Session lifecycle messages (SESSION_INIT, SESSION_ACCEPT, SESSION_UPDATE, SESSION_CLOSE)
"chat" — Chat messages and streaming LLM output
"audio" — Real-time audio stream
"video" — Real-time video stream
"ops/{req-id}" — Request/response operations (one track per request)

section.t: Protocol bindings add prefix-scoped tracks to enable multiple protocols to operate concurrently within a single session without track name collisions:

li.t: "ext/{proto}/{category}/{id}" — Custom protocol extensions, where {proto} identifies the protocol

section.t: For example, the MCP over MOQT specification defines tracks like (mcp, {session-id}, tools) -- ({tool-name}); within PACE, this maps to track name "mcp/tools/{tool-name}" under the agent's session namespace, preserving the MCP semantics while coexisting with A2A or other protocol tracks in the same session.
See for concrete examples of agent-to-agent, agent-to-tool, and multi-agent collaboration workflows.

section.name: Session Discovery Namespace
section.t: Agents advertise their active sessions on this top-level discovery namespace so that other agents can find sessions to join. Each agent publishes one track per active session (the track name is the session-id). Each object on a session track contains:

li.t: session-id — The shared session UUID
description — Human-readable purpose of the session
participants — List of agent-ids currently in the session
modalities — Supported data modalities (text, audio, video, etc.)

section.t: Agents discover active sessions by issuing SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE on ("pace", "discovery", "sessions").

section.name: Session Management
section.t: A PACE session represents a logical communication context between two or more agents. Sessions provide lifetime management, context preservation, and failure recovery. All session operations use the namespace structure defined in .

section.name: Session Lifecycle
section.t: Sessions progress through defined states:

figure.name: Session State Machine
figure.artwork: IDLE ──establish──▶ PENDING ──accept──▶ ACTIVE ◀──update──┐ ◀──reject──────────┘ │ │ │ suspend terminate │ ▼ │ │ SUSPENDED ▼ │ │ │ CLOSED ◀──┘ │ └resume──▶ ACTIVE └─timeout──▶ CLOSED

dd.t: No session exists. Agent is available to initiate or accept sessions.
Establishment in progress (negotiation, authentication).
Session established; data exchange occurring. May be updated.
Temporarily inactive, state preserved. Transitions to CLOSED on timeout.
Session terminated. Resources released.

section.name: Session Establishment
section.t: Session establishment creates a shared communication context between two or more agents. Its goals are: (1) negotiate capabilities and modalities both agents support, (2) exchange identity tokens and verify authorization, and (3) set up the MOQT namespace subscriptions so that both agents can publish and receive messages within the session.

The mechanism relies on three MOQT operations. The initiator publishes a SESSION_INIT object on a new session control track under its own namespace, containing proposed session parameters. It then delivers a lightweight invite to the target agent's inbox track, notifying the target that a session is waiting. The target agent inspects the invite, subscribes to the initiator's session namespace to read the SESSION_INIT parameters, and — if it accepts — publishes a SESSION_ACCEPT on its own session control track. The initiator then subscribes to the target's session namespace, completing the bidirectional subscription setup.
Once both agents have subscribed to each other's session namespace, the session transitions to ACTIVE and data exchange can begin on any track within that session scope.

figure.name: Session Establishment Example
figure.artwork:
Session Establishment Example:
Agent A MOQT Relay Agent B │ │ │ │── PUBLISH SESSION_INIT ─────────▶│ │ │ Track: ("pace","agents", │ │ │ "agent-a",{sid}) -- "ctrl" │ │ │ Object: {session params, │ │ │ capabilities, modalities} │ │ │ │ │ │── PUBLISH invite ───────────────▶│── forward to B's inbox ───────▶│ │ Track: ("pace","agents", │ │ │ "agent-b") -- "inbox" │ │ │ Object: {session-id, │ │ │ from: agent-a} │ │ │ │ │ │── PUBLISH session advertisement ▶│ │ │ Track: ("pace","discovery", │ │ │ "sessions","agent-a") │ │ │ -- {sid} │ │ │ │ │ │ │ [B receives invite, reads │ │ │ SESSION_INIT, decides to │ │ │ accept] │ │ │ │ │ │◀── SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE ────────│ │ │ ("pace","agents","agent-a", │ │ │ {sid}) │ │ │ │ │ │◀── PUBLISH SESSION_ACCEPT ─────│ │◀── forward ─────────────────────│ Track: ("pace","agents", │ │ │ "agent-b",{sid}) -- "ctrl" │ │ │ Object: {capabilities, │ │ │ accepted modalities} │ │ │ │ │── SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE ──────────▶│ │ │ ("pace","agents","agent-b", │ │ │ {sid}) │ │ │ │ │ │◀═══════════ PACE Session ACTIVE ═══════════════════════════════▶│

section.name: Session Parameters
section.t: The SESSION_INIT object contains:

li.t: session-id: Globally unique session identifier (UUID)
session-type: Short-lived (bounded duration) or long-lived (indefinite)
session-timeout: Maximum idle duration before automatic termination
max-participants: Maximum number of agents in the session
supported-modalities: Bitmask of data modalities the agent can handle
identity-token: Agent identity token (see )
supported-protocols: Application protocols offered (A2A, MCP, etc.)

section.name: MOQT Setup Extensions
section.t: PACE defines the following MOQT setup parameters negotiated during CLIENT_SETUP/SERVER_SETUP:

tr.td: Agent identity token or certificate reference

section.name: Timed Sessions
section.t: Sessions are either short-lived (bounded duration, auto-terminates on completion or timeout) or long-lived (indefinite, survives idle periods via SUSPENDED state). The session-timeout parameter defines the maximum idle period before automatic transition to CLOSED.

section.name: Session Update
section.t: Active sessions can be updated by publishing a SESSION_UPDATE message on the control track. Updates can modify modalities, participants, authorization scopes, or timeout. All participants MUST acknowledge the update before new parameters take effect.

section.name: Session Recovery
section.t: PACE provides graceful recovery from network and server failures:

dd.t: Sessions survive network path changes (e.g., WiFi to cellular) via QUIC's connection ID mechanism without re-establishing the MOQT session.
Relays cache recent objects, allowing reconnecting agents to receive missed messages without requiring peer retransmission.

Agents resume SUSPENDED sessions by reconnecting to the relay, re-issuing PUBLISH_NAMESPACE on their agent namespace, and re-subscribing to peer session namespaces. The relay delivers cached objects from the point of disconnection.
Agents SHOULD periodically publish state checkpoints on a dedicated track, enabling recovery after relay failures.

section.name: Session Termination
section.t: Sessions terminate explicitly via SESSION_CLOSE on the control track or implicitly via timeout. Upon termination, all subscriptions are cancelled, pending operations receive cancellation notifications, and session resources are released after a configurable grace period.

section.name: Agent Identity Model
section.t: PACE authenticates agents independently of the users they represent. This enables independent revocation, capability-scoped permissions, audit trails for agent actions, and delegation chains.

section.name: Agent Identity Token
section.t: Each agent presents an identity token during session establishment. The token format is based on JWT with agent-specific claims:

tr.td: Identity provider that issued the token
User or organization the agent serves

section.t: The token is cryptographically signed by the issuing authority. Agents MAY use the SD-JWT based identity mechanism defined in to support selective disclosure of identity attributes during session establishment.

section.name: Delegation Chains
section.t: When an agent acts on behalf of another agent, the identity token includes a delegation-chain field tracing the authorization path (e.g., User → Coordinator → Researcher → Tool). Each entry records the granting agent and the scope granted. Receiving agents verify the complete chain to ensure each link has appropriate authorization.

section.name: Agent Discovery
section.t: Agents discover each other using MOQT's PUBLISH_NAMESPACE and SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE operations before establishing any PACE session. Discovery operates on the Agent Namespace scope defined in . Each agent is identified by a globally unique agent-id (UUID), verifiable via the Agent Card (see ).

section.name: Part 1: Discovering Agent Namespaces
section.t: Agents announce their presence by issuing PUBLISH_NAMESPACE on their namespace ("pace","agents",{agent-id}). Other agents discover available peers by issuing SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE on the common prefix ("pace","agents"). The relay forwards namespace announcements to matching subscribers, enabling Agent B to learn Agent A's namespace prefix without prior knowledge.
If an agent-id is known out-of-band (e.g., from a registry or URL), agents MAY skip Part 1 and proceed directly to Part 2.

section.name: Part 2: Fetching Agent Card and Inbox
section.t: Once Agent B knows Agent A's namespace prefix, it issues SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE on ("pace","agents",{agent-a}) to discover A's tracks ("card", "inbox"). Agent B then subscribes to the "card" track to fetch A's Agent Card (capabilities, identity, authentication) and learns the "inbox" track where session invitations can be delivered.

section.name: Agent Card
section.t: Each agent publishes an Agent Card on track "card" under its namespace ("pace","agents",{agent-id}). When capabilities change, the agent publishes a new object (incrementing the group). Receivers SHOULD verify the card's signature and expiration before acting on its claims.
All Agent Cards MUST include:

li.t: Agent identifier (UUID) and display name
Supported modalities and protocols
Authentication schemes
Identity claims (issuer, public key, expiration)

section.t: The card format is protocol-specific. For A2A agents, see . Agent Cards MAY use selective disclosure to reveal only claims necessary for a given interaction.

section.name: Inbox Track
section.t: Each agent subscribes to its own inbox track ("pace","agents",{agent-id}) -- "inbox" upon connecting to the relay. Other agents publish session invitations to this track. Each inbox object contains a session-id and the initiator's agent-id. Late-joining agents receive cached inbox messages from the relay.

section.name: Multi-Modal Data Exchange
section.t: PACE supports concurrent exchange of multiple data modalities within a single session, each with appropriate quality of service.

section.name: Modality Types
section.t: PACE defines the following data modality classes:

section.name: Channel Architecture
section.t: Each modality maps to dedicated MOQT tracks within the Session Communication Namespace (). Different modalities are isolated by track name while sharing session context and authorization.

section.name: Priority and Quality of Service
section.t: MOQT's 0-255 priority scale enables differentiated treatment of messages based on urgency and modality. PACE defines the following priority tiers:

section.name: Group Order
section.t: MOQT Group Order controls delivery sequencing within a track:

li.t: Real-time media: Descending order (newest first, drop stale frames)
Chat/streaming text: Ascending order (preserve message sequence)
Operations: Ascending order (preserve execution order)
Bulk transfers: Ascending order (sequential chunk delivery)

section.name: Request/Response Pattern
section.t: Request/response interactions use coordinated publish operations. Agent A publishes a request object on its own track ("pace","agents","agent-a",{sid}) -- "ops/{req-id}". Agent B, which has subscribed to A's session namespace, receives the request, processes it, and publishes the response on its own corresponding track ("pace","agents","agent-b",{sid}) -- "ops/{req-id}". Agent A receives the response through its subscription to B's session namespace.

section.name: Streaming Pattern
section.t: Long-running operations produce incremental results as MOQT objects organized into groups representing execution phases. The server advances to a new group at each phase transition (e.g., initialization, progress, completion). Multiple objects within a group represent incremental data for that phase.
Late-joining subscribers receive the latest complete group from relay cache, enabling mid-operation catch-up without replaying the full history.

section.name: Real-Time Media Exchange
section.t: Audio and video streams use dedicated tracks ("audio", "video") with descending group order (newest-first) and high priority (32-63), ensuring media frames preempt lower-priority data under congestion.

section.name: Communication Topologies
section.t: PACE supports multiple communication topologies through MOQT's relay fan-out:

dd.t: Two agents publish and subscribe to each other's session tracks. Used for tool invocation, task delegation, and bilateral collaboration.
One agent publishes; multiple agents subscribe. The relay handles fan-out without the publisher maintaining per-subscriber state. Used for broadcast notifications and shared context distribution.

All participants publish on their own tracks and subscribe to each other's tracks within the same session-id. Adding a participant requires publishing SESSION_JOIN on the control track; existing participants receive the notification and subscribe to the new agent's session namespace.

A coordinator creates child PACE sessions to delegate subtasks. Each level operates as a separate session with narrowed authorization scope. Delegation chains () maintain an auditable path from the original user authorization.

section.name: Authorization Model
section.t: PACE implements a behavior-driven authorization model where access tokens are scoped to specific operations an agent is permitted to perform.

section.name: Behavior-Driven Scopes
section.t: Scopes are structured as {domain}:{resource}:{action}:{constraints}, bound to specific agent behaviors rather than roles. Constraints support dynamic limits (time bounds, resource limits, counts).

section.name: Delegated Authorization
section.t: When agents invoke other agents, each delegation narrows the scope. Agent A (holding scope S) requests a sub-scope S' ⊂ S for Agent B. Agent B can further narrow to S'' ⊂ S' for downstream tools. Downstream agents cannot exceed their delegator's permissions.
Authorization tokens are presented in SESSION_INIT and validated including the full delegation chain. Tokens are refreshed proactively before expiration.

section.name: Confirmation and Evidence
section.t: For high-risk operations, PACE supports confirmation requirements where agents must present cryptographic evidence of approval (human, policy-check, or MFA) before the operation proceeds.

section.name: Transport Security
section.t: All PACE communication is encrypted via TLS 1.3 (QUIC requirement). Agent identity tokens are cryptographically signed with short expiry. MOQT Common Access Tokens provide relay-level namespace authorization. Relay nodes cannot access payload content unless explicitly authorized as trusted intermediaries.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Agents SHOULD minimize shared data to what is necessary for the task. Long-lived sessions SHOULD support forward secrecy through periodic key rotation. Relay operators MUST NOT retain content beyond operational necessity.

section.name: MOQT Transport Binding Layer
section.t: This section defines how PACE maps to MOQT primitives: connection setup, namespace operations, message serialization, and operation mappings. All namespace and track references follow the structure defined in .

section.name: Connection Establishment
section.t: Agents MUST establish either a native QUIC connection or a WebTransport session as defined in . For native QUIC connections, agents MUST use the ALPN value "moqt". For WebTransport, the protocol is negotiated using the "WT-Available-Protocols" mechanism as specified in .
Upon establishing the MOQT session (CLIENT_SETUP / SERVER_SETUP), an agent performs the bootstrap sequence to make itself discoverable and ready to receive session invitations. This sequence is:

li.t: Announce: PUBLISH_NAMESPACE on ("pace", "agents", {agent-id})
Publish Agent Card: Publish on track "card" under its namespace
Subscribe to inbox: Subscribe to its own "inbox" track

section.t: See for the full discovery flow that follows bootstrap.

section.name: Track Organization
section.t: Each agent publishes exclusively on its own tracks. Other agents subscribe to tracks they are interested in. The relay handles fan-out to all subscribers. This per-agent publishing model ensures clear ownership and enables relay caching.
Namespace structure and track names are defined in . Participants discover each other's session tracks using SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE on ("pace", "agents", {peer-agent-id}, {sid}).

section.t: Protocol messages are encapsulated within MOQT objects using a PACE envelope prepended to the payload:

section.t: Custom protocols extend this binding by defining additional track subcategories, custom message schemas within JSON-RPC params, protocol-specific priorities, and custom MOQT extension headers. Implementations SHOULD document extensions and MAY register them in the IANA PACE Protocol Binding Registry.

section.name: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns
section.t: Common coordination patterns built on PACE sessions and MOQT fan-out:

dd.t: Each agent subscribes to its predecessor's response track and publishes to the next agent's request track, forming a pipeline.
A coordinator publishes a single request; relay fan-out delivers it to all subscribing specialists. Results are published back to tracks the coordinator subscribes to.
Agent A publishes a HANDOFF message on the control track. Agent B subscribes to the task track, receives cached context from the relay, and continues execution without explicit state transfer.
Coordinators create child PACE sessions for sub-task delegation. Delegation chains ensure authorization propagates through the hierarchy (see ).

section.name: Scalability and Reliability
section.t: PACE inherits MOQT's relay architecture for geographic distribution and load management:

li.t: Subscription Aggregation: Multiple subscribers to the same track result in a single upstream subscription, reducing origin load
Geographic Locality: Edge relays cache content close to subscribers, minimizing round-trip latency
Fault Isolation: Relay failures are localized; other paths continue operating

section.name: Failure Modes and Recovery
section.t: Session recovery mechanics are defined in .

section.name: Threat Model
section.t: PACE considers the following threats:

li.t: Unauthorized agents joining sessions or impersonating legitimate agents
Man-in-the-middle attacks on agent communications
Privilege escalation through delegation chain manipulation
Denial of service via excessive session creation or message flooding
Data exfiltration through compromised relay nodes
Hallucination-driven operations by compromised or malfunctioning agents
All transport is encrypted via TLS 1.3 (QUIC requirement)
Agent identity tokens are cryptographically signed with short expiry
Delegation chains are validated end-to-end at each hop
Relay authorization via MOQT Common Access Tokens restricts namespace access
Rate limiting at relay nodes prevents flooding
Confirmation requirements for high-risk operations prevent hallucination-driven damage
Session timeout and explicit termination prevent resource exhaustion

section.name: Relay Trust Model
section.t: MOQT relays are trusted for routing but not content inspection. Relay operators:

li.t: MUST NOT inspect or modify message payloads
MUST enforce namespace-level access control
MUST implement rate limiting and abuse prevention
MAY cache objects for operational efficiency
MUST NOT retain cached content beyond operational necessity

section.t: For end-to-end confidentiality from relay operators, agents MAY implement payload encryption above the PACE layer.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs

abstract.t: Many protocols make use of points of extensibility that use constants to identify various protocol parameters. To ensure that the values in these fields do not have conflicting uses and to promote interoperability, their allocations are often coordinated by a central record keeper. For IETF protocols, that role is filled by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

To make assignments in a given registry prudently, guidance describing the conditions under which new values should be assigned, as well as when and how modifications to existing values can be made, is needed. This document defines a framework for the documentation of these guidelines by specification authors, in order to assure that the provided guidance for the IANA Considerations is clear and addresses the various issues that are likely in the operation of a registry.
This is the third edition of this document; it obsoletes RFC 5226.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

abstract.t: This document defines the core of the QUIC transport protocol. QUIC provides applications with flow-controlled streams for structured communication, low-latency connection establishment, and network path migration. QUIC includes security measures that ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability in a range of deployment circumstances. Accompanying documents describe the integration of TLS for key negotiation, loss detection, and an exemplary congestion control algorithm.

front.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

abstract.t: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol. TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.
This document updates RFCs 5705 and 6066, and obsoletes RFCs 5077, 5246, and 6961. This document also specifies new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations.

JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. The claims in a JWT are encoded as a JSON object that is used as the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS) structure or as the plaintext of a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) structure, enabling the claims to be digitally signed or integrity protected with a Message Authentication Code (MAC) and/or encrypted.

This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). HTTP/2 enables a more efficient use of network resources and a reduced perception of latency by introducing header field compression and allowing multiple concurrent exchanges on the same connection. It also introduces unsolicited push of representations from servers to clients.
This specification is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax. HTTP's existing semantics remain unchanged.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

front.title: HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol

abstract.t: This document describes HTTP Datagrams, a convention for conveying multiplexed, potentially unreliable datagrams inside an HTTP connection.

In HTTP/3, HTTP Datagrams can be sent unreliably using the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. When the QUIC DATAGRAM frame is unavailable or undesirable, HTTP Datagrams can be sent using the Capsule Protocol, which is a more general convention for conveying data in HTTP connections.
HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol are intended for use by HTTP extensions, not applications.

section.name: Example Workflows
section.t: This appendix illustrates common PACE workflows end-to-end, showing how agents use the namespace structure, session establishment, and protocol bindings defined in this document.

section.name: Agent-to-Agent: Task Delegation
section.t: Agent A (a coordinator) delegates a research task to Agent B. This is a point-to-point session using the A2A binding.
Setup: Agent A generates session-id s1 (a UUID) and establishes a session with Agent B via the flow in .
Resulting namespace layout:
section.artwork:
Agent A publishes: ("pace","agents","agent-a","s1") -- "ctrl" (SESSION_INIT) ("pace","agents","agent-a","s1") -- "a2a/request/r1" (task request)
Agent B publishes: ("pace","agents","agent-b","s1") -- "ctrl" (SESSION_ACCEPT) ("pace","agents","agent-b","s1") -- "a2a/response/r1" (task result)
section.t: Flow:

li.t: A publishes SESSION_INIT on its "ctrl" track and sends an invite to B's inbox
B accepts, subscribes to A's session namespace, publishes SESSION_ACCEPT on its own "ctrl" track
A subscribes to B's session namespace
A publishes a JSON-RPC request on "a2a/request/r1": {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"message/send","params":{...},"id":"r1"}
B receives the request (via its subscription to A's namespace), processes it, and publishes the result on "a2a/response/r1"
A receives the response via its subscription to B's namespace
Either agent publishes SESSION_CLOSE on "ctrl" to terminate

section.name: Agent-to-Tool: MCP Tool Invocation
section.t: Agent A needs to read a file using a filesystem tool (an MCP server).
Setup: Agent A generates session-id s2 and establishes a session with the filesystem tool.
Resulting namespace layout:
section.artwork:
Agent A publishes: ("pace","agents","agent-a","s2") -- "ctrl" ("pace","agents","agent-a","s2") -- "mcp/tools/readFile" (tool call)
Tool publishes: ("pace","agents","fs-tool","s2") -- "ctrl" ("pace","agents","fs-tool","s2") -- "mcp/tools/readFile" (tool result)
section.t: Flow:

li.t: A establishes a session with the tool (SESSION_INIT / ACCEPT)
Tool receives the call, reads the file, publishes the result on its own "mcp/tools/readFile" track
A receives the file contents
A may issue additional tool calls within the same session or close it

section.name: Multi-Agent Collaboration
section.t: Agent A (coordinator) creates a research session and invites Agent B (web researcher) and Agent C (data analyst) to collaborate.
Setup: Agent A generates session-id s3, invites B and C via their inbox tracks.
Resulting namespace layout:
section.artwork:
Agent A publishes: ("pace","agents","agent-a","s3") -- "ctrl" (session mgmt, assignments) ("pace","agents","agent-a","s3") -- "chat" (coordination messages)
Agent B publishes: ("pace","agents","agent-b","s3") -- "ctrl" (SESSION_ACCEPT) ("pace","agents","agent-b","s3") -- "chat" (status updates) ("pace","agents","agent-b","s3") -- "a2a/task/research-1" (findings)
Agent C publishes: ("pace","agents","agent-c","s3") -- "ctrl" (SESSION_ACCEPT) ("pace","agents","agent-c","s3") -- "chat" (status updates) ("pace","agents","agent-c","s3") -- "a2a/task/analysis-1" (results)
section.t: Subscriptions: Each agent subscribes to the other two agents' session namespaces:

li.t: A subscribes to ("pace","agents","agent-b","s3") and ("pace","agents","agent-c","s3")
B subscribes to ("pace","agents","agent-a","s3") and ("pace","agents","agent-c","s3")
C subscribes to ("pace","agents","agent-a","s3") and ("pace","agents","agent-b","s3")

section.t: Flow:

li.t: A establishes session, B and C accept
A publishes task assignments on "chat" — the relay fans out to both B and C
B performs web research, publishes findings incrementally on "a2a/task/research-1" (using MOQT groups for phases)
C subscribes to B's research track, receives findings as they arrive, and begins analysis
C publishes analysis results on "a2a/task/analysis-1"
A monitors all progress through its subscriptions and publishes a final summary when complete
A publishes SESSION_CLOSE — all participants unsubscribe

section.name: Agent-to-Tool with Streaming: Long-Running Operation
section.t: Agent A invokes a code-generation tool that produces output incrementally.
Setup: Same as tool invocation — Agent A and the tool share session-id s4.
Flow:

li.t: A publishes a tool call on "mcp/tools/generateCode"
Tool begins generating code and publishes results using MOQT groups:
Group 0: {"status":"started","language":"python"}
Group 1, Object 0: first code block
Group 1, Object 1: second code block
Group 2: {"status":"complete","totalLines":142}
A receives objects as they are published (ascending group order)
If A needs to cancel, it publishes a cancellation on "ctrl"
Tool receives cancellation, stops generation, publishes final status
